Ontario trillium benefit 2026–27: how rent, age and income set each part, and whether to wait for one June payment

Work through the three credits inside the Ontario trillium benefit with CRA’s 2026 calculation sheets, see why only 20% of rent counts and why age 64 matters, and price the choice between monthly payments and one payment in June 2027.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Estimate the three parts of a 2026–27 Ontario trillium benefit and compare monthly payments with one June payment

The central idea

The Ontario trillium benefit is three credits paid together: the energy and property tax credit, the sales tax credit and, in the north, the Northern Ontario energy credit. For July 2026 to June 2027 they are based on 2025 rent or property tax, age on 31 December 2025 and 2025 family income. Rent counts at only 20%, people 64 or older get a much higher property tax component, and the sales tax credit fades fastest as income rises. Waiting for a single June payment pays the same total and gives up only a little interest; it is a budgeting choice.

01

One deposit, three credits

Many Ontario households see a deposit labelled “Ontario trillium benefit” around the 10th of each month and treat it as one payment. CRA’s Province of Ontario page describes it as the combined payment of three separate credits, each with its own rules:

  • Ontario energy and property tax credit (OEPTC), for people who paid rent or property tax on their main home in Ontario, or who lived in a public or non-profit long-term care home, on a reserve or in a designated student residence.
  • Ontario sales tax credit (OSTC), which needs no housing cost at all, and is paid for each adult and each child in the family.
  • Northern Ontario energy credit (NOEC), only for people who lived in Northern Ontario on 31 December and paid rent, property tax or a similar housing cost there.

The payments from July 2026 to June 2027 are based on the 2025 return, filed in spring 2026, and on Form ON-BEN for the energy and property tax credit and the northern credit. That one-year lag matters for planning: a pay rise in 2026 does not change these payments, but it will change the ones starting in July 2027. This guide follows each credit through CRA’s 2026 calculation sheets and then looks at the one real choice the benefit offers, how it is paid.

02

Energy and property tax credit: why only part of your rent counts

CRA’s 2026 OEPTC sheets start from an occupancy cost: 20% of rent paid for 2025, plus property tax paid for 2025. Rent counts at one fifth, so CAD 10,000 of rent counts the same as CAD 2,000 of property tax.

The credit then has two parts. The energy component is the occupancy cost up to CAD 290. The property tax component is a base amount plus 10% of the occupancy cost, with that 10% capped, and never more than the occupancy cost itself:

  • Under 64 on 31 December 2025: CAD 73 plus 10% of occupancy cost, with the 10% capped at CAD 944. The highest total, CAD 1,307, needs an occupancy cost of CAD 9,440, which is rent of about CAD 47,200 a year.
  • 64 or older (for a couple, if either spouse was): CAD 617 plus 10%, with the 10% capped at CAD 581. The highest total, CAD 1,488, is reached at an occupancy cost of CAD 5,810, or rent of about CAD 29,050.

The third chart draws both lines. At CAD 12,000 of rent a year, the credit before any income reduction is CAD 603 under 64 and CAD 1,147 at 64 or older; the senior sheets are worth nearly twice as much on the same rent. The credit is then reduced by 2% of adjusted family net income above CAD 29,047 for a single person under 64 with no children, CAD 36,309 for a family under 64 or a single senior, and CAD 43,571 for a senior family. A “family” on these sheets means a spouse or common-law partner, or a single parent with the sole care of a child; parents who share care use separate sheets that split the amounts.

03

Sales tax credit and the northern credit

The OSTC pays up to CAD 378 for each adult and each child in the family for July 2026 to June 2027, up from CAD 371 a year earlier. It falls by 4% of adjusted family net income above CAD 29,047 for a single person with no children, or above CAD 36,309 for a single parent or a couple. A single person’s OSTC therefore ends at about CAD 38,500 of income, while a couple with two children keeps some credit until about CAD 74,100. The OSTC is the only part that does not depend on housing costs, so someone living with parents who pays no rent can still receive it.

The NOEC is CAD 189 for a single person with no children and CAD 290 for a family, for residents of districts including Algoma, Cochrane, Kenora, Manitoulin, Nipissing, Parry Sound, Rainy River, Sudbury, Thunder Bay and Timiskaming. CRA’s 2026 NOEC sheets reduce it by only 1% of income above CAD 50,833 (single) or CAD 65,356 (family), so it is often the last part of the benefit left as income rises.

The second chart shows all three for the inputs you enter, across income. Where the OEPTC and OSTC are both falling, each extra CAD 1,000 of 2025 income costs CAD 60 of benefit the following year, before income tax. The benefit phase-out guide shows how such reductions stack with tax on a pay rise, and the federal Groceries and Essentials Benefit guide covers the federal credit that phases out over a similar income range.

04

Three worked households

All three use CRA’s 2026 sheets as summarised above, before any rounding CRA applies.

  1. Single renter in Toronto, age 35 (the default). Rent CAD 24,000 for 2025, income CAD 35,000. Occupancy cost CAD 4,800; energy component CAD 290; property tax component CAD 73 + CAD 480 = CAD 553. Income is CAD 5,953 above the CAD 29,047 threshold, so the OEPTC falls by CAD 119.06 to CAD 723.94, and the OSTC falls by CAD 238.12 to CAD 139.88. Total CAD 863.82, about CAD 71.99 a month.
  2. Senior couple who own a home in Sudbury. Property tax CAD 4,200, income CAD 48,000, both 64 or older. Energy component CAD 290; property tax component CAD 617 + CAD 420 = CAD 1,037. The OEPTC is reduced by 2% of CAD 4,429 to CAD 1,238.42. The OSTC on two adults (CAD 756) falls by 4% of CAD 11,691 to CAD 288.36. Income is below the CAD 65,356 family NOEC threshold, so the full CAD 290 applies. Total CAD 1,816.78.
  3. Family of four in Thunder Bay with income of CAD 80,000. Rent CAD 24,000. The OEPTC ends at about CAD 78,460 of income and the OSTC at about CAD 74,110, so both are zero. The NOEC is CAD 290 minus 1% of CAD 14,644, or CAD 143.56, paid in one July payment because the year’s total is CAD 500 or less.

A senior homeowner may also qualify for the Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant, up to CAD 500, which the senior sheets subtract in part from the OEPTC. That step is not in the calculator.

05

Monthly or one June payment

CRA pays the year’s entitlement in twelve monthly payments on the 10th, starting 10 July 2026, moved earlier to the last working day when the 10th falls on a weekend or holiday. Three rules change that, according to CRA and Ontario pages for the 2026 benefit year:

  • If the annual total is CAD 500 or less, it is paid in one payment in the first month, usually July.
  • If the annual total is more than CAD 2 but no more than CAD 10, CAD 10 is paid; CAD 2 or less is not paid.
  • If the total is over CAD 500 and you chose on the 2025 return to wait, it is paid in one payment on 10 June 2027. Ontario notes the total is the same either way.

The fourth chart shows what waiting costs. In the default case, CAD 71.99 a month saved at 2.5% until June would be worth CAD 873.67, so the single payment gives up about CAD 9.85 of interest. For the senior couple above, it is about CAD 20.72. Waiting does not raise the benefit; it only changes when the cash arrives.

That makes the June option a budgeting tool. Someone who pays a large annual bill in late spring, such as property tax instalments or home insurance, may prefer one payment they will not spend. Someone with a tight monthly budget is usually better off with the monthly amount and a separate savings plan; the annual bills sinking-fund guide shows how to set money aside each month for once-a-year costs, and the child benefit calendar lays out other monthly deposits.

06

What to check before relying on the estimate

  • You must file, and apply. The OSTC is assessed from your return; the OEPTC and NOEC also need Form ON-BEN completed with your 2025 rent or property tax. Missing the form means no OEPTC even with high rent. CRA’s OTB questions and answers cover who in a couple applies and how shared accommodation is reported.
  • Status is fixed at 31 December 2025. Marital status, age 64 and northern residence are taken at that date for the whole benefit year. A move out of Ontario, a death, or a change in the care of a child can change or stop later monthly payments.
  • Income is “adjusted family net income”. That is net income for both spouses, with some adjustments CRA makes, not take-home pay. RRSP deductions lower it; RRSP and RRIF withdrawals raise it. The GIS withdrawal-timing guide shows the same one-year lag for seniors.
  • Amounts are set each year. The 2027 benefit year will use new figures. Check CRA’s child and family benefits calculator or your notice for your actual amount.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart shows maximum amounts published by the Government of Ontario for the 2026 benefit year, reviewed 27 October 2026. The other charts apply the formulas on CRA’s 2026 calculation sheets (page details 30 July 2026) to hypothetical editable inputs. OSTC: CAD 378 per adult and child, reduced by 4% above CAD 29,047 (single, no children) or CAD 36,309 (family); CAD 371 and CAD 28,506 / CAD 35,632 a year earlier.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · 2026 Ontario energy and property tax credit (OEPTC) calculation sheets ↗

    Index page dated 20 January 2026; individual sheets dated 30 July 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026.   3. Canada Revenue Agency · 2026 Northern Ontario energy credit (NOEC) calculation sheets ↗

    Index page dated 20 January 2026; individual sheets dated 30 July 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. CAD 189 for a single person with no children reduced by 1% above CAD 50,833; CAD 290 for a family reduced by 1% above CAD 65,356; shared-care sheets split the two.
